articles.headline: Ensilage and Silos.
articles.text:
So much has been written and said lately on the subject of ensilage and silos, that it has attracted especially the attention of small stockmen to the benefits to be derived from their use. To anyone wishing a ready means of fattening cattle or who have any number of milch cows, silos undoubtedly would prove a profitable investment.

From "A Practical Treatise on Ensilage and Silos," by E. W. Ross & Co. of Springfield, Ohio, we learn many points of interest. The work consists almost wholly in letters, written by farmers and others who have tested the value of ensilage and all are loud in their praises of it.

As is to be expected, opinions differ widely as to details, but we publish as nearly as possible, the substance of the letters.

Like most other things, silos cost almost any amount the owner wishes. Aside from the lumber, or stone and cement required, the item of labor is the only expense. Thus, good silos for feeding a few animals, have been built for from $30 to $50. More elaborate ones, for feeding a larger number of animals, could easily cost thousands of dollars. The only requisites seem to be: water and air-tight sides and bottom and a movable top that will fit inside the walls as perfectly as possible. Sometimes the top consists only of hay or straw. The silo is usually built partly underground, as it is then handier, both to fill and empty. Common dimensions for a silo are twenty feet long, ten feet deep and twelve feet wide. Such a one, built of lumber in this country, with double walls filled with dirt, would cost about $250. Figuring at fifty pounds to the cubic foot, such a silo would hold about sixty tons. This will last twenty cows for six months.

Opinions vary as much in ensilage as they do in silos. Clover of different kinds, pea vines, etc., are highly recommended, but the vast majority seem to be in favor of corn. This is cut when the corn is in the milk, the ears and stalks are cut into lengths about an inch long and the silo is filled as quickly as possible. The ensilage is tramped thoroughly and the top is then put on. Over this is spread earth or rocks, about a foot thick. There must be a constant and heavy pressure and the top of the silo must be movable, so that it will follow the ensilage, which shrinks a third or more. The ensilage ferments and is ready to be fed at the end of two or three months. As to its relative value, we quote an estimate from one of the letters. "With one hundred fresh milch cows, feed for six months will take 250 tons of timothy hay, worth at least $7 per ton, $1,750. It will take at the same time 132 tons of bran and meal, at $14 a ton, $1,850. This makes a total cost, under the old system, of $3,600. Now, for the same time and number of cows, with ensilage; 450 tons of ensilage, cost in silo under the press, $450; fifty tons of timothy hay, at $7 per ton, $350; seventy-two tons of bran and meal, at $14 per ton, $1,000, making a total of $1,800. We feed fifty pounds of ensilage, seven to eight pounds of mill-feed and five pounds of hay per day to each cow. Here is a gain of $1,800 in favor of ensilage. And not only this, but we gain in milk from one and one-half to two quarts a day from each cow, which will make about $1,000 more to add to the gain in feed." Of course the feed which makes milk in a cow, would make fat in a steer. A fair to good crop of corn ensilage ranges from fifteen to twenty tons to the acre.

We predict that before many years, silos will be built numerously, throughout the range country. An ever-occurring possibility of fire, either before or after mowing his hay, the liability of that feed being extremely scarce and of poor quality, and the impossibility of any more than keeping an animal in condition on hay alone, will inevitably turn the ranchman's attention to ensilage. It is a sure crop, costs but little, if any, more than hay, is three times as valuable as hay and cannot burn, either before or after cutting.
articles.summary: Editorial summarizing a treatise on silos and ensilage and predicting silos will spread through the range country.

articles.text: The project of the establishment of a fattery here by the Ref. Car Co., is now approaching realization. Every one of the sixteen members of the committee from the Montana association, agreed individually to put in cattle of their own and as a body, agreed to report the matter favorably to the Association. The details of the plan here have not been fully worked out, but in the rough, are as follows: The plant will consist of a barn, capable of holding 2,500 cattle or upwards, besides outside ranches, for holding the cattle, a large farm for raising a root crop, etc. Between September and December, 18,000 cattle will be delivered here for fattening. Fifteen or sixteen thousand of these will be distributed to the different ranches, to be held ready for the fattening process. From two to three thousand will be fattening all the time. Over 250 acres of land on the river bottom will be cultivated for a root crop, which will be fed not only to keep the cattle in condition, but it will also be a constituent of the fattening food. The boiled roots, costing only a few cents a hundred pounds will take the place of corn-meal costing a dollar a hundred. The analysis of brewers' grain is as follows: Fat, 6.57; Albuminoids, 20.92; Carbo hydrates, 56.33; Cellulose; 12.12; Mineral matter, 4.06; Total, 100. Under very unfavorable circumstances last winter, such as being fed in a nearly open shed, exceptionally cold weather and several mistakes in feeding, made by new men, three steers were fed twelve quarts of the brewers' grain and five pounds each of hay per day and averaged a gain of three pounds each per day between January 7 and March 6. The last week of the experiment, when the weather had moderated, the cattle gained five pounds a day. From careful estimates, it is found that brewers' grain can be put on the market for about half a cent a pound. It will, if the supply of grain holds out, revolutionize the feeding system of the United States. Prof. Mott of New York, after a careful test, pronounces the new food to be practically and scientifically correct and highly recommends its use. There seems now no reason to doubt that the fattery here will be a great and constantly increasing success. The Northern Pacific railroad is joining actively with the Marquis in the fattery enterprise and gives rates on the brewers' grain which are merely nominal.
articles.summary: The Refrigerator Car Co.'s cattle fattery at Medora nears realization with Montana stockmen's backing and Northern Pacific support for the Marquis.

articles.text: From a Galveston, Texas, press report, we learn that "Thousands of beef cattle are being brought to Galveston by rail, to be started on the trail. There are thousands of cattle and a thousand head of horses leaving every day, the cattle for Dakota and the horses for Kansas. Water and grass are exceedingly scarce in western Texas, owing to the drought and cattle that passed a good winter, are going to market in very poor condition. The trail is now virtually open and fully 45,000 head of cattle are going northward. Heretofore, most of the cattle from the ranches, struck the trail in the southern or western part of the state. This year, the long drought in the Pecos valley, has forced cattlemen to send their herds as far as possible by rail, before starting them on the trail. This had never been attempted before, as cattlemen thought it would cost too much. The reverse has been the case. Instead of the customary losses of cattle on the trail before they get out of the state, there is none at all. Leading cattlemen here, looking after the interests of their herds, express the opinion that there will be no national trail in a few years, as railroad transportation from Texas to Dakota, Montana and Colorado will be found cheaper."
articles.summary: Reprinted Galveston report on Texas cattle being shipped by rail before taking the trail north to Dakota.

articles.text:
The Little Missouri River Stockgrowers' Association at its last meeting, passed a resolution adopting the Montana law in respect to the time of branding cattle. As the law seems to be little known, we publish it in full: "It shall be unlawful for any person to brand or mark any calf or other cattle that are running at large during the first day of August and the first day of September of each year, and between the fifteenth day of November and the fifteenth day of the month of May following. Provided, that the owner of any stock may brand, on his own premises, at any time, in the presence of two responsible citizens:

Any person violating the provisions of this act shall be guilty of a misdemeanor, and, on conviction before any court of competent jurisdiction, shall be punished by a fine not less than twenty-five dollars, nor more than one hundred dollars, for each and every animal thus branded, or by imprisonment in the county jail for a term not exceeding six months, or may be punished by both such fine and imprisonment, in the discretion of the court."

Of course the penalty in the above law cannot be inflicted in Dakota, but it is a good law, the breaking of which would cause more disputes and hard feeling than almost anything else in the cattle business.
articles.summary: The Little Missouri River Stockgrowers' Association adopts the Montana law on branding seasons; the law is printed in full.

The section reads as follows: "Every person who willfully discharges any species of fire-arms, air-gun or other weapon, or throws any other missile in any public place, where there is any person to be endangered thereby, although no injury to any person shall ensue, is guilty of a misdemeanor.

articles.text: Charlie Rowe and Miss Bentley, both of Beaver creek, were married at Dickinson, May 2. We join in hearty congratulations to the newly married couple. We prophecy that this union will cause renewed activity to the social life of the Beaver valley.
articles.summary: Charlie Rowe and Miss Bentley of Beaver creek were married at Dickinson May 2.

articles.text: Arnett & Thomas are making some valuable additions to the AHA herd. Already they have driven on their range, about thirty head of full-blood Hereford bulls. Two thousand two-year-old Montana steers have also been bought and will be added to their herd this summer.
articles.summary: Arnett & Thomas add Hereford bulls and 2,000 Montana steers to the AHA herd.

articles.text: The largest barn in the world is situated at Papilion, Neb. It covers five acres of land and shelters 3,750 cattle. It is said to be the intention to enlarge this stable to accommodate 8,000 cattle. The object is to take range cattle and finish them into fine beef. This great barn is said to have a complete system of waterworks and is thoroughly washed, twice every day. The cattle are fed on cooked meal. One man feeds the whole herd by turning on a large faucet, thus letting the feed run to them from tanks.—[Hoof and Horn.
articles.summary: Reprint from Hoof and Horn on a huge cattle-finishing barn at Papillion, Nebraska.

articles.text: Lieutenant Partello of Fort Keogh, has not lost his grip a particle on shooting. With a military gun and plain open sights he recently made a perfect score of fifteen consecutive bull's-eyes at 500 yards and seventy-three out of a possible seventy-five at 600 yards. The target-practice of his company is also improving rapidly. They made seventy qualifying scores a few days ago, where a good average is fifteen. The Lieutenant will make the Bad Lands a visit in a few months.
articles.summary: Lieutenant Partello of Fort Keogh, a crack rifle shot, will visit the Bad Lands in a few months.

articles.text: The average importation of horses from Canada into the United States for some years past has been about 22,000 head. A few years ago, the average value of horses so imported, per head, was $95; whereas last year, it was $140. This shows not only a rapid improvement in the quality of the supply, but the fact that the demand requires just as many, is evidence that it is at least just as easy, and in many cases far easier, to find purchasers for the better class of animals. The difference to Canada, represented in these values, is over $1,000,000 annually.—[Hoof and Horn.
articles.summary: Reprint from Hoof and Horn on rising values of horses imported from Canada.

articles.headline: Perfect Gun Sights.
articles.text: In the BAD LANDS COW BOY this week will be observed the advertisement of Lyman's gun sights, which are probably about as near perfect as will be reached in this century. His rear sights are universally used by hunters and riflemen throughout Europe and America, and, when used with his new ivory bead front sight which is here illustrated, an ordinary marksman can bore the bulls-eye with astonishing accuracy, and kill running game with ease. The American Field recently published engravings of targets made with these sights, showing that out of seventeen shots, all struck within the bulls-eye but one, which struck the line between bulls-eye and center. We have received a sample of the sight, and will take pleasure in showing it.
articles.summary: Editorial notice praising Lyman's gun sights; a sample is on view at the Cow Boy office.

articles.text: Dave. Brown and wife of Mingusville, accompanied Mr. and Mrs. Tisdale to Medora. They returned home Tuesday evening.
articles.summary: Dave Brown and wife of Mingusville accompanied the Tisdales to Medora and went home Tuesday.

articles.text: Pierre Wibaux and his brother were in town Monday. The latter, whose home is in France, is visiting Wibaux at his Beaver Creek ranch.
articles.summary: Pierre Wibaux and his brother from France were in town Monday.

articles.text: W. J. Tomkins' daughter has returned from her Tongue river trip. She started to-day for her fathers' ranch, where she intends to spend the summer.
articles.summary: W. J. Tomkins' daughter is back from the Tongue river and has gone to her father's ranch for the summer.

articles.text: Jas. Boyd of Deadwood, came up from the Hills Monday and started back Tuesday with one of the M. S. & F. Co's. stages. He will use it on a new line between Deadwood and the Carbonate camp.
articles.summary: Jas. Boyd of Deadwood took one of the M. S. & F. Co.'s stages for a new Deadwood-Carbonate camp line.

articles.text: Ed. Turner, Al. Uhlrich and George Myers, started yesterday morning for the O'Fallon creek round-up, which begins at Hockett's ranch on May 25. The two former represent the Ref. Car Co. and the latter, the Maltese Cross.
articles.summary: Ed. Turner, Al. Uhlrich and George Myers left for the O'Fallon creek round-up, Myers representing the Maltese Cross.

articles.text: Will some one who knows explain whether it is grubs, heel-flies or what it is, that worry cattle now? A number have been noticed who with no apparent reason will start on a dead run as though they had a job carrying the mail.
articles.summary: The editor asks why cattle are suddenly stampeding, perhaps from grubs or heel-flies.

articles.text: John Goodall, who was in the Black Hills country, selling horses for the Ref. Car Co., has been instructed by telegraph to return as soon as possible, bringing with him the unsold horses. He will probably be here inside of a week.
articles.summary: John Goodall has been recalled from the Black Hills with the Ref. Car Co.'s unsold horses.

articles.text: Tom. Crisswell, a well-known and well-liked cowboy, who was a foreman for Driskill's outfit in the Black Hills country, died in Buckholtz, Texas, recently, of paralysis. We also learn that a cowboy named Cox, died at the VVV ranch recently.
articles.summary: Deaths of cowboy Tom Crisswell in Texas and a cowboy named Cox at the VVV ranch.

articles.text: Vic. Smith went through Medora last Sunday, on his way to Billings, where he will make his headquarters. While on the platform here, he carefully wore a plug hat under his arm. He has been making a great reputation throughout the east this winter, exhibiting his skill in the use of the rifle.
articles.summary: Rifle exhibition shot Vic. Smith passed through Medora on his way to Billings.

articles.text: Yesterday morning, Mr. and Mrs. Jack Tisdale stepped from the cars and were soon busy accepting the congratulations of their numerous friends. Both are well known here and god-speeds follow them from every side. The marriage ceremony took place at Mingusville Tuesday evening.
articles.summary: Newly married Mr. and Mrs. Jack Tisdale arrived at Medora after their wedding at Mingusville.

Sheriff's Sale.

[First publication May 6.]

TER. OF DAKOTA, COUNTY OF MORTON, To which county Billings county is attached for judicial purposes. } SS.

Notice is hereby given that by virtue of a judgment and decree in foreclosure, rendered and given by the District Court of the sixth judicial district, in and for the county of Morton, (to which county Billings county is attached for judicial purposes,) and Territory of Dakota, and filed in the office of said court, on the 23rd. day of April, A. D. 1886, in an action wherein the Northern Pacific Refrigerator Car Company is plaintiff and John Kiefer and Mary J. Kiefer are defendants, in favor of said plaintiff, and against said defendant, for the sum of One thousand three hundred and twenty-seven dollars and fifty-three cents ($1,327.53,) the principal and interest secured by a certain mortgage, given by John Kiefer and Mary J. Kiefer, his wife, to the Northern Pacific Refrigerator Car Company, together with interest thereon from April 10th., A. D. 1886, the date of said decree and also the cost of said plaintiff, taxed at the sum of ninety-one dollars and thirty-five cents, ($91.35,) which judgment and decree directed the sale by me of the real estate hereinafter described, to satisfy the amount of said judgment, with interest thereon, and costs and expenses of said sale, or so much thereof as the proceeds of such sale, applicable thereto, will satisfy, and by virtue of a writ issued out of the office of the Clerk of said court, in and for said county of Morton, to which county, Billings county is attached for judicial purposes, and under the seal of said court, directing me to sell said real property, pursuant to said judgment and decree,

I, George W. Harmon, Sheriff of said Morton county and the person appointed by said court to make said sale, will sell the hereinafter described real estate to the highest bidder, for cash, at public auction, at the front door of the Court House in the city of Mandan, in the county of Morton, (to which county Billings county is attached for judicial purposes,) and Territory of Dakota, on the 17th day of June, A. D. 1886, at two o'clock, P. M., of that day, to satisfy said judgment, interest and costs, and the costs and expenses of such sale, or so much thereof as the proceeds of such sale, applicable thereto, will satisfy.

The premises to be sold as aforesaid, pursuant to said judgment and decree, and to said writ, and to this notice, are described in said judgment, decree and writ, as follows, to-wit:

All those tracts or parcels of land lying and being in the County of Billings, and Territory of Dakota, described as follows:

Lots number Thirteen (13) and Fourteen (14) in Block number nine (9,) as laid down and designated on the plat of the town of Medora, Billings county, D. T., as the same is recorded in the office of Register of Deeds of Morton county, D. T., to which County Billings county, which is unorganized, is attached for judicial purposes.

Dated at Mandan, Dakota, April 29, A. D., 1886.

GEORGE W. HARMON, Sheriff,
Morton County, Dakota.

EDWARD S. ALLEN, Plaintiff's Att'y.

D. 1886, before me, a Notary Public in and for said County and State, personally appeared Julius LeMoyne and in his own name and for himself and in the name of his constituent John A. Wills, and in due form of law, acknowledged the within instrument of writing to be his act and deed and the act and deed of his constituent, the said John A. Wills, to the end that the same be recorded as such.

Witness my hand and notarial seal, the day and year aforesaid.

T. F. BIRCH,
[Notarial Seal.] Notary Public.

STATE OF PENNSYLVANIA, County of Allegheny. } ss.

On this 30th. day of April, A. D., 1886, before me, a Notary Public in and for said County and State, personally aapeared W. A. Nicholson, Edward E. Phelps, Charles H. Bradley, Pennock Hart, William Wade, Trustee, M. Fundenberg, Joseph U. Rose, M. C. Byrnes, Thomas H. Hartley, Webster Gray, Frak Shanley, Howard Hartley, Trustee and S. I. Boggs and in due form of law acknowledged the within instrument of writing to be their act and deed, to the end that the same be recorded as such.

Witness my hand and notarial seal the day and year above written.

HENRY C. LYON,
[Notarial Seal.] Notary Public.

TERRITORY OF DAKOTA, County of Morton. } ss.

On this 4th. day of May, A. D., 1886, before me, a Notary Public in and for said County and Territory, personally appeared H. T. Hallock, to me personally known to be the same person described in and who executed the foregoing instrument and acknowledged to me that he executed the same for the uses and purposes therein expressed.

[Notarial Seal.] ELBRIDGE C. COOKE,
Notary Public,
Dakota Ter.
